description.summary: Reranking applies a second scoring step to reorder retrieved candidates before context assembly.
description.description: Reranking is a RAG technique that rescores an initial candidate set before context assembly. Its effectiveness and operational impact depend on the first-stage retriever, evaluation domain, reranker model, candidate depth, hardware, deployment, and inference strategy.
description.problemStatement: Initial retrieval may return a broad candidate set whose top order is not aligned with the final generation need.
description.coreIdea: Score retrieved candidates with an additional ranking method and pass the reordered subset to context assembly.

evidence.summary: The paper reports that its BERT passage reranker exceeded the previous state of the art on MS MARCO passage retrieval by 27 percent relative in MRR@10.
evidence.interpretation: This is a measured benefit for one historical BERT system and benchmark setup, not an estimate of the gain from reranking in other pipelines.
limitations: The result is limited to the reported BERT reranker and MS MARCO passage retrieval task.
The 27 percent value is relative to the paper's historical state-of-the-art baseline and uses MRR@10.
The abstract does not establish transfer to other first-stage retrievers, candidate depths, model families, hardware, or inference implementations.
The experiment evaluates passage retrieval rather than downstream RAG generation quality.

evidence.summary: BEIR evaluated ten lexical, sparse, dense, late-interaction, and reranking systems on eighteen heterogeneous datasets and found reranking and late-interaction systems best on average for zero-shot effectiveness.
evidence.interpretation: The benchmark supports considering reranking when zero-shot retrieval effectiveness across heterogeneous domains is the decision criterion, subject to the evaluated system set and costs.
limitations: The average covers the eighteen BEIR datasets and ten retrieval systems evaluated in the paper, not all domains or current systems.
An average result can hide dataset-specific regressions and does not provide a universal ranking for every domain.
Effectiveness depends on the evaluated architecture, first-stage retrieval setup, and candidate depth.
The benchmark evaluates retrieval effectiveness rather than downstream RAG generation quality.

evidence.summary: The BEIR abstract characterizes the evaluated reranking and late-interaction systems as achieving strong average zero-shot effectiveness at high computational cost.
evidence.interpretation: Effectiveness and computational expense must be evaluated as separate decision dimensions; the source does not justify assigning every reranker a fixed cost level.
limitations: The high-cost characterization applies to the architectures and BEIR evaluation represented by the paper.
The abstract does not provide a hardware-normalized cost that transfers across deployments.
Actual compute, latency, and monetary cost depend on model family, candidate count, rerank depth, hardware, batching, implementation, and inference strategy.
The study reports retrieval evaluation rather than end-to-end RAG generation cost or quality.

evidence.summary: The paper reports average zero-shot BEIR nDCG@10 of 0.532 for monoT5-3B reranking BM25's top 1000 candidates and 0.490 for SGPT-5.8B, a difference of 0.042 corresponding to the paper's more-than-four-average-points finding.
evidence.interpretation: The result demonstrates a measurable zero-shot advantage for the evaluated monoT5-3B reranking pipeline over SGPT-5.8B; it does not establish superiority over every first-stage retriever, bi-encoder, or reranker.
limitations: The comparison is between monoT5-3B reranking 1000 BM25 candidates and the SGPT-5.8B bi-encoder, not two otherwise identical pipelines.
The more-than-four-point result is an average over the zero-shot BEIR datasets excluding MS MARCO and can mask domain-level variation.
Transfer depends on the BM25 first stage, top-1000 candidate depth, model families, and domains not seen during MS MARCO fine-tuning.
The result does not directly measure latency, hardware-dependent compute, or downstream RAG generation quality.

evidence.summary: For BM25 top-1000 reranking, monoT5-60M, monoT5-220M, and monoT5-3B scored 0.356, 0.381, and 0.398 MRR@10 on in-domain MS MARCO, while their average zero-shot BEIR nDCG@10 scores were 0.425, 0.478, and 0.532.
evidence.interpretation: The larger observed scaling gains on zero-shot BEIR than on in-domain MS MARCO make model size a domain-dependent choice rather than a uniform effectiveness lever.
limitations: The finding is bounded to monoT5 sizes of 60M, 220M, and 3B parameters, MS MARCO fine-tuning, and the evaluated BEIR domains.
Both in-domain and zero-shot monoT5 results rerank the top 1000 BM25 candidates, so the same scaling pattern is not established for other first-stage retrievers or depths.
MS MARCO uses MRR@10 while BEIR uses nDCG@10; the comparison concerns within-context scaling trends rather than direct equality of metric values.
Larger-model costs and latency remain hardware-, implementation-, batching-, and deployment-dependent.
The tests measure retrieval effectiveness rather than downstream RAG generation quality.

evidence.summary: On TREC DL19-DL23, the paper compares DeBERTa-v3-large and ELECTRA-large rerankers over SPLADE-v3, SPLADE-v3-DistilBERT, and SPLADE-v3-Doc at top-50, top-100, and top-200 depths and reports that which reranker is better varies by dataset in nDCG@10.
evidence.interpretation: The observed lack of a consistent in-domain winner means reranker rankings should not be generalized without recording the first-stage variant, dataset, and rerank depth.
limitations: The finding is specific to TREC DL19-DL23, three SPLADE-v3 first-stage variants, and the DeBERTa-v3-large and ELECTRA-large rerankers.
The paper evaluates top-50, top-100, and top-200 depths and reports no statistical significance tests, so difficult to distinguish does not mean proven equivalence.
Results can change outside the evaluated nDCG@10 datasets, model families, rerank depths, implementation, and hardware.
The comparison evaluates retrieval effectiveness rather than downstream RAG generation quality.

evidence.summary: Across BEIR, BEIR-12, and LoTTE, the paper's mean nDCG@10 comparisons show different results for DeBERTa-v3-large versus ELECTRA-large and for top-50, top-100, and top-200 reranking over the three SPLADE-v3 variants.
evidence.interpretation: Out-of-domain reranker choice must be evaluated jointly with the first-stage SPLADE variant and rerank depth; a result at one depth or on one collection does not establish a depth-independent ordering.
limitations: The finding is bounded to three SPLADE-v3 variants, two cross-encoder model families, top-50/100/200 depths, and the evaluated BEIR and LoTTE collections.
ArguAna behaved anomalously, so the paper reports both BEIR and BEIR-12 without ArguAna; neither aggregate establishes one optimum across all domains.
Latency, compute, and cost depend on candidate count, model family, implementation, batching, hardware, deployment, and inference strategy.
The evaluation measures retrieval effectiveness rather than downstream RAG generation quality.

inputRequirements.name: Retrieved candidates
inputRequirements.description: A candidate set returned by an upstream retrieval stage.

outputArtifacts.name: Reranked candidates
outputArtifacts.description: A reordered candidate set prepared for context assembly.

implementationConsiderations: Choose the candidate pool and rerank depth together because scoring more candidates can change effectiveness, latency, and compute use.
Evaluate model family, model size, batching, hardware, deployment, and inference strategy before assigning an operational impact.
Preserve first-stage retrieval scores and reranker scores when possible so changes in candidate recall can be distinguished from changes in ordering.
evaluationGuidance: Record the first-stage retriever, its candidate pool size, and the number of candidates passed to and retained after reranking.
Record the reranker model family and model size, including inference and deployment choices that affect comparisons.
Compare against a named baseline on a specified dataset and domain using the same effectiveness metric and candidate pool.
Report in-domain and out-of-domain results separately rather than relying only on an average across domains.
Measure end-to-end latency and compute or resource use alongside retrieval effectiveness, with hardware and batching context.
When the consumer is a RAG pipeline, evaluate selected-context and downstream generation outcomes separately from retrieval ranking metrics.
